pos: n. (proper name; the man from whom Omri bought the hill of Samaria)
etymology: Hebrew Shemer, probably from shamar, to keep or watch. The city built on his hill is Shomeron in Hebrew, which the Authorized Version renders Samaria.
biblical_def: One verse holds everything Scripture says of him: “And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria” (1 Kings 16:24). Omri had reigned six years in Tirzah (1 Kings 16:23) and wanted a capital he could fortify. He paid Shemer two talents of silver and named the new city after the seller. The Authorized Version uses Shemer twice in the one verse and never again. The dictionary notes what his hill became. Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom for two hundred years, the seat of Ahab and Jezebel, the city where the temple of Baal stood, the city Elijah and Elisha walked into and out of, and the city Assyria took in the sixth year of Hezekiah. The Chronicler's verdict on the man who bought it is given in the next verse: “But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him” (1 Kings 16:25). A farmer sold a hill for silver and his name went on the most notorious city in Israel.

Where political-success metrics and the inspired verdict conflict, the dictionary follows the inspired verdict.

pos: n. (proper name; parent of one of the servants who killed King Joash of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Shim'ath, from shama', to hear. 2 Chronicles 24:26 identifies the bearer of the name as an Ammonitess.
biblical_def: Shimeath is named in the record of a royal assassination: “For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him, and he died; and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David” (2 Kings 12:21). The Chronicler adds the detail the book of Kings leaves out — Shimeath was an Ammonitess, and the parallel names Zabad for Jozachar (2 Chronicles 24:26). The Authorized Version uses Shimeath twice. The dictionary notes the motive the Chronicler supplies, because it is the key to the whole reign: the servants conspired “for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Chronicles 24:25). Joash had been saved as an infant by Jehoiada, crowned by him, and guided by him; and after Jehoiada died Joash had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the court of the house of the LORD. Two servants, one of them the son of an Ammonite woman, killed the king on his bed for that murder. He was buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings. A man is not kept by a godly mentor; he is kept by grace, and Joash outlived his mentor and apostatised.

pos: n. (proper name; two men — a father of one of Joash's assassins, and a son of Heber of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Shomer, the active participle of shamar, to keep or watch — literally a keeper.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version gives the name to two men. The first is the father of a regicide: “For Jozachar the son of Shimeath, and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, smote him” (2 Kings 12:21). The Chronicler's parallel at 2 Chronicles 24:26 names Jehozabad's mother Shimrith a Moabitess, and the margin notes or, Shomer — so the two accounts may name the father and the mother of the same man. The second Shomer is an Asherite: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32). The Hebrew means keeper, the participle of the verb that stands behind the great question of Genesis 4 — am I my brother's keeper? — and behind the blessing of Numbers 6: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee. The dictionary follows the Authorized Version in letting one headword cover both men, and notes the irony the name carries in its first bearer's household: a man called Keeper whose son killed the king he was set to guard.

pos: n. (proper name; Joab's armourbearer, one of David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Nachray, of uncertain meaning, possibly from a root for snorting or for a stream. He is called a Beerothite in Samuel and a Berothite in Chronicles.
biblical_def: Naharai is listed near the end of the roll of David's mighty men: “Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah” (2 Samuel 23:37), with the parallel at 1 Chronicles 11:39. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. Two things about the entry he occupies are worth weight. He is identified entirely by whose armour he carried — the armourbearer of Joab — and he stands in the list immediately after Zelek the Ammonite and two names before Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 23:39). David's thirty-seven included an Ammonite and a Hittite. The dictionary notes both facts. Beeroth was a Gibeonite city, which means Naharai belonged to the people Joshua had spared by a treaty won through deceit, and he ended up carrying the shield of Israel's commander. Scripture keeps the roll of the men who held other men's armour, and it keeps the foreigners in the roll without apology. The kingdom of David had Gentiles in its order of battle, which is the shape of the kingdom of David's greater Son.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite of Gibeah, father of Ittai of David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Ribay, probably from rib, to contend or plead a cause — the word for a legal controversy.
biblical_def: Ribai is named only as a father: “Heleb the son of Baanah, a Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai out of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin” (2 Samuel 23:29), with the parallel “Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, that pertained to the children of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 11:31). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes where he came from. Gibeah of Benjamin is a place with a history: the town of the Levite's concubine and the atrocity of Judges 19, after which the tribe of Benjamin was nearly destroyed; and afterwards Gibeah of Saul, the home town of the king David replaced. A man of Gibeah, of the tribe of Saul, in the roll of David's mighty men. Benjamin had every reason to resent the house of David, and Shimei of Benjamin cursed David on the road from Jerusalem. Ribai's son fought for him. Scripture does not comment, but the fact is in the list, and the dictionary draws the obvious point: God gathers servants out of the towns with the worst records and the strongest grievances.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Meholah — the designation of Adriel, Saul's son-in-law)
etymology: Hebrew Mecholathi, the gentilic of Abel-Meholah, probably the Abel-meholah of Judges 7:22 in the Jordan valley.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice and both times of one family. First the marriage: “But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” (1 Samuel 18:19). Saul had promised Merab to David and gave her to Adriel instead — the first of the manoeuvres by which Saul tried to keep David from the throne and from his house. Then the accounting, years later: the Gibeonites demand satisfaction for Saul's slaughter of their people, and “the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite” (2 Samuel 21:8). Five of Adriel's sons were hanged before the LORD in Gibeah. The Authorized Version uses Meholathite in these two verses alone. The dictionary notes the arc. A marriage arranged to spite David ended with the sons of that marriage dying for the sins of the man who arranged it — Saul's broken oath to the Gibeonites, visited on his house.

corruption_summary: 2 Samuel 21 is charged as collective punishment; Scripture presents it as satisfaction for a broken national oath sworn in the name of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The hanging of Saul's descendants is one of the hardest narratives in Scripture, and the modern charge is that innocent men died for another's crime. The text supplies the frame: a famine, an enquiry of the LORD, and the answer of 2 Samuel 21:1 — it is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Israel had sworn to that people in the name of the LORD, and Saul had broken the oath. National covenants bind nations and their houses, which is the same principle by which Achan's household fell and by which all men die in Adam.

The principle to recover is the seriousness of a sworn oath. Joshua's treaty was obtained by deceit and God still held Israel to it four centuries later. A promise made in the name of the LORD is not voided by the other party's bad faith.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Azubah, the mother of Jehoshaphat)
etymology: Hebrew Shilchi, probably from shalach, to send. He is known only as the grandfather of a king.
biblical_def: Shilhi is named twice, in two accounts of one reign, and both times only as a grandfather: “Jehoshaphat was thirty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi” (1 Kings 22:42), repeated almost word for word at 2 Chronicles 20:31. The Authorized Version uses the name in these two verses alone. The dictionary notes the convention this verse belongs to, because it is one of the quiet complementarian witnesses of Scripture. The formula for every king of Judah gives the king's age, the length of his reign, and his mother's name. The queen mother is named for good kings and bad — Azubah for Jehoshaphat, Athaliah for Ahaziah, Nehushta for Jehoiachin — because the woman who raised the king mattered to the chronicle of the kingdom. Shilhi is in the Bible because his daughter raised a king who “walked in the way of Asa his father, and departed not from it, doing that which was right in the sight of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 20:32). Three generations are in the verse, and the one that is named least did the work.

The royal formula answers it: every king of Judah is introduced with his mother's name, in a document that never bothers to name most of the kings' wives. The chronicle thought the woman who raised the king was part of the public record of the kingdom.

Azubah is named for raising Jehoshaphat, and Shilhi is in the Bible for being her father. The creational order of headship and submission does not diminish a mother's labour; it is the frame in which Scripture records it.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah who married Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh)
etymology: Hebrew Mered, from marad, to rebel. The name means rebellion.
biblical_def: Mered is named twice, in two consecutive verses of a Judahite genealogy: “And the sons of Ezra were, Jether, and Mered, and Epher, and Jalon” (1 Chronicles 4:17), and then the detail that makes him memorable — “And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). A man of the tribe of Judah married a daughter of Pharaoh. The Authorized Version gives no narrative, no date, and no comment. The dictionary notes what the Chronicler does supply: her name. Bithiah is a Hebrew name meaning daughter of Jehovah, which is not what an Egyptian princess is called at home. Somewhere behind these two verses is a conversion, and the Chronicler records the new name without telling the story. The man's own name means rebellion; the wife's means daughter of the LORD. The dictionary draws the restrained conclusion the text allows: Scripture keeps the names of Gentiles brought into the covenant people, as it keeps Rahab and Ruth, and the line of Judah has an Egyptian princess in it.

pos: n. (proper name; two men of Judah — a brother of David, and a son of Jerahmeel)
etymology: Hebrew Otsem, probably from a root meaning to be strong.
biblical_def: Ozem is named twice, of two different men in the same chapter. The first is a brother of David: “Ozem the sixth, David the seventh” (1 Chronicles 2:15). The second is a son of Jerahmeel: “And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1 Chronicles 2:25). The Authorized Version uses the name twice and tells us nothing more of either man. The dictionary notes what the first verse settles. The Chronicler lists seven sons of Jesse, with David seventh; 1 Samuel 16 has Samuel pass over seven and send for the youngest, and 1 Samuel 17 names only three of the brothers who went to the war. Scripture gives the household from different angles for different purposes, and the Chronicler's purpose is the royal line. Ozem is in the Bible as the sixth son of Jesse, which means he was one of the sons Samuel looked at and the LORD refused, before the sheep were sent for. “For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

corruption_paragraphs: The differing counts of Jesse's sons between 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles are regularly set down as contradiction. They are lists made for different ends: Samuel narrates the anointing and counts the sons present, Chronicles gives the royal genealogy and counts the household. Neither claims to be the other.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Nadab of the house of Jerahmeel, who died childless)
etymology: Hebrew Seled, probably from a root meaning to leap or to exult.
biblical_def: One verse, and the whole of it is an epitaph: “And the sons of Nadab; Seled, and Appaim: but Seled died without children” (1 Chronicles 2:30). The Authorized Version uses the name twice in that single verse and never again. The dictionary notes how unusual the clause is. A genealogy exists to trace descent; a man who leaves no descendants is a dead end, and no ordinary family register would bother to record him. Scripture records him, and records why he stops. The Chronicler does the same for Jether a few verses later and for the daughters of Zelophehad in Numbers. This is the honesty of inspired genealogy: it keeps the men whose lines end. For the Hebrew mind childlessness was the heaviest of sorrows — Hannah's grief, Rachel's, Abraham's long waiting — and the Chronicler neither hides it nor explains it. The dictionary adds the New Testament's word to it, which is for every believer whose name will end with him: “Neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree” (Isaiah 56:3), for God gives such a man a name better than of sons and of daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.

corruption_paragraphs: The modern treatment of childlessness runs to two extremes: it is either a private misfortune no one may mention, or it is reframed as an equally good choice. Scripture does neither. It names the sorrow plainly — Seled died without children, Hannah wept, Rachel said give me children or else I die — and it holds children to be a blessing and a heritage from the LORD.
